name: Freexya – Cookie Consent, SMTP, Redirects & Security Toolkit
author: nexya

sections.description:
One plugin for the jobs every WordPress site needs, instead of five or six:

  • E-mails that do not arrive — send through SMTP or an API, keep a log of every message, and read the server’s own reason when one fails.
  • A cookie banner that really blocks — third-party scripts and embeds wait for consent, with Google Consent Mode v2.
  • 404s after a redesign — a log of the broken addresses visitors hit, with their count, redirected in one click.
  • Security — HTTP headers, a limit on failed logins, and your plugins checked against known vulnerabilities.

Each job is a module you switch on from the hub, and a module that is off registers nothing: none of its hooks run on the site. The modules:

  • Dashboard — a readable admin home and a tidied toolbar.
  • Shortcuts — duplicate content, reorder it by hand, add entries in one click.
  • Roles & capabilities — capabilities sorted under the post type that creates them, and the site seen through a role’s eyes without leaving your own account.
  • Activity log — who changed what, with the before and the after.
  • Cookies — a consent banner, third-party scripts held back until consent, and a scan that finds them.
  • SEO — titles and descriptions with a suggestion drawn from the page’s text, sitemap, schema, llms.txt.
  • Mail — SMTP, an API provider, or a Gmail or Microsoft 365 account connected with OAuth, a delivery log, a test message, an invisible captcha for the site’s forms.
  • Redirects — exact redirects and a 404 log with the hit count.
  • Media — regenerate thumbnails in the background, in batches.
  • Security — security headers, a content policy, a limit on failed logins, and a check of the installed plugins against known vulnerabilities.
  • Maintenance — a holding page, database clean-up, a database export, and the previous version of each extension kept before its update.
  • Custom fields — field groups with repeaters, flexible content and relations, kept in their own tables, and content types and taxonomies of your own.
  • Element — sixteen Elementor widgets for custom fields, NCF’s or ACF’s: repeaters as cards, tabs or tables, galleries and sliders, key figures, teams, timelines, taxonomies, maps.
  • Translate — your site in several languages: each page linked to its translations, a translation editor beside the original (blocks, Elementor, ACF and NCF fields), addresses in /en/, a menu per language, a language switcher, hreflang, and every text of the site translated from the admin. A site coming from WPML or Polylang moves over in one click.

Free and Pro

Everything above is free, on as many sites as you like. nexya Pro, sold on nexya.dev, adds three modules — nexya forms, Mailya for newsletters and a page cache — and the parts that do the repetitive work for you: suggested redirects and pattern rules, CSV import, a daily vulnerability pass and a file fingerprint with rollback, a two-step login, updates undone by themselves when they break the site, undo from the activity log, a second sending server and failure alerts for mail, a branded login screen and admin skin, banner appearance and consent service by service, scheduled database clean-up, orphan image sizes, folders in the media library, and longer log retention. The free version contains none of that code; nexya Pro is delivered by Freemius after purchase, and takes over from this plugin with the same settings.

Privacy

The plugin sends nothing to a third party by default. The features that reach the network, and what they send, are listed under External services below.

Multisite

Multisite networks are not supported. On a network the plugin stays switched off and says so.

External services

Nothing below runs unless you switch the matching module or option on. No data leaves the site by default, and the plugin sends no usage data anywhere.

WPVulnerability (Security module, vulnerability watch). When you start a check from the Security screen, the plugin asks the public WPVulnerability API whether the installed plugins have known vulnerabilities. For each installed plugin, its slug is sent to www.wpvulnerability.net; nothing else about the site is sent. Nothing is sent until you start a check. Terms and privacy (legal notice of its publisher): https://www.robotstxt.es/legal/

WordPress.org checksums (Security module). While the Security module is on, once a day and when you press “Check now”, the plugin asks api.wordpress.org — the same service WordPress uses for its own updates — for the checksums of the installed WordPress version, sending only that version number and the site language, then compares them with the core files on your server. Terms: https://wordpress.org/about/privacy/

IndexNow (SEO module, optional, off by default). Only if you switch it on, each time a page is published, updated or taken down its address is sent to api.indexnow.org, which shares it with the search engines that take part (Bing, Yandex, Seznam, Naver and others), along with the site’s host name and the verification key the plugin serves at the root of your site. Nothing is sent while the site asks search engines not to index it, or runs on a local address. Terms: https://www.indexnow.org/terms — Privacy (Microsoft, which runs the IndexNow service): https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/privacy/privacystatement

Stripe (nexya forms, Payment module, optional, nexya Pro). Only once you switch the module on and enter your own Stripe secret key, a form with a payment field sends, when the visitor submits it, the amount, the currency, the name of the form, the visitor’s e-mail address if the form asks for one, and the entry’s number to api.stripe.com to open a Stripe Checkout page; the visitor then pays on Stripe’s site. Stripe calls back the site’s own webhook address to confirm the payment. Terms: https://stripe.com/legal/ssa — Privacy: https://stripe.com/privacy

PayPal (nexya forms, Payment module, optional, nexya Pro). Only once you enter your own PayPal REST app credentials, a form with a payment field sends, when the visitor chooses PayPal, the amount, the currency, the name of the form and the entry’s number to api-m.paypal.com (or api-m.sandbox.paypal.com in sandbox mode) to open a PayPal approval page; the visitor approves the payment on PayPal’s site, and the site captures it when they come back. Terms: https://www.paypal.com/legalhub/home — Privacy: https://www.paypal.com/myaccount/privacy/privacyhub

Patchstack (Security module, optional). Only if you enter your own Patchstack API key, the same check also asks api.patchstack.com, sending each installed plugin’s slug and your key. Terms: https://patchstack.com/terms-and-conditions/ — Privacy: https://patchstack.com/privacy-policy/

E-mail delivery (E-mails module). When you pick an API provider instead of SMTP, the messages your site sends are handed to that provider’s API: sender, recipients, subject, body and attachments, at the moment the message is sent. You choose the provider and enter its API key. The providers offered are Brevo (https://www.brevo.com/legal/termsofuse/ — https://www.brevo.com/legal/privacypolicy/), SendGrid (https://www.twilio.com/en-us/legal/tos — https://www.twilio.com/en-us/legal/privacy), Postmark (https://postmarkapp.com/terms-of-service — https://postmarkapp.com/privacy-policy), Resend (https://resend.com/legal/terms-of-service — https://resend.com/legal/privacy-policy), SMTP2GO (https://www.smtp2go.com/terms/ — https://www.smtp2go.com/privacy/), MailerSend (https://www.mailersend.com/legal/terms-of-service — https://www.mailersend.com/legal/privacy-policy), SendLayer (https://sendlayer.com/terms-of-service/ — https://sendlayer.com/privacy-policy/), Mandrill (https://mailchimp.com/legal/terms/ — https://mailchimp.com/legal/privacy/), Mailgun (https://www.mailgun.com/legal/terms/ — https://www.mailgun.com/legal/privacy-policy/), Elastic Email (https://elasticemail.com/resources/usage-policies/terms-of-use — https://elasticemail.com/resources/usage-policies/privacy-policy) and SparkPost (https://www.sparkpost.com/policies/tou/ — https://www.sparkpost.com/policies/privacy/).

Gmail and Microsoft 365 sending (E-mails module, optional). Only if you choose Google (Gmail, Workspace) or Microsoft 365 (Outlook) as the sending method and connect an account. When you press “Connect”, your browser goes to accounts.google.com or login.microsoftonline.com, where you sign in and allow the site to send e-mail; the plugin then sends the authorisation code it gets back, with the client ID and secret you entered, to oauth2.googleapis.com or login.microsoftonline.com to obtain an access token, and renews that token there when it expires while the site is sending. No password is stored on the site. Each message the site sends then goes through smtp.gmail.com, or smtp.office365.com / smtp-mail.outlook.com, with its sender, recipients, subject, body and attachments, at the moment it is sent. Google — Terms: https://policies.google.com/terms — Privacy: https://policies.google.com/privacy. Microsoft — Terms: https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/servicesagreement — Privacy: https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/privacy/privacystatement

Cloudflare (Cache module, optional). Only if you switch the Cloudflare option on and enter your zone ID and API token: each time the nexya cache is emptied, the plugin asks api.cloudflare.com to empty the cache of that zone, sending the zone ID, the token and, when only some pages changed, their addresses. Terms: https://www.cloudflare.com/terms/ — Privacy: https://www.cloudflare.com/privacypolicy/

Form webhook (nexya forms, optional). Only if you enter an address in a form’s settings, each entry of that form is sent, when it is submitted, to that address as JSON: the form’s name and number, the entry’s number and date, the page it was sent from, the site’s address, and the answers with the label and type of each field. You choose the address (Zapier, Make, n8n, a CRM…); the plugin contacts no address you did not enter, and the terms and privacy policy that apply are those of the service you chose.

AI suggestions (optional). The plugin calls no AI provider itself. When you press a button that asks for a suggestion (a title, a description, an image text…), the text needed for it is handed to the AI client built into WordPress, which sends it to the provider of the connector you set up in WordPress, under that provider’s terms. Without such a connector, these buttons do not appear and nothing is sent.

Audience measurement tags (SEO module). If, and only if, you enter an ID or an address for one of them, the module prints that service’s tag on the front end; the visitor’s browser then loads the script from the service and sends it what that tag collects.
* Google Tag Manager and Google Analytics 4, from www.googletagmanager.com. Terms: https://marketingplatform.google.com/about/analytics/terms/us/ — Privacy: https://policies.google.com/privacy
* Plausible, from plausible.io or the address you enter. Terms: https://plausible.io/terms — Privacy: https://plausible.io/privacy
* Umami, from the address of your own Umami instance or Umami Cloud. Terms: https://umami.is/terms — Privacy: https://umami.is/privacy
* Matomo, from the address of your own Matomo instance or Matomo Cloud. Terms: https://matomo.org/matomo-cloud-terms-of-service/ — Privacy: https://matomo.org/privacy-policy/

Freemius (trial and purchase of nexya Pro). The Freemius SDK ships with the plugin in anonymous mode: on its own it sends nothing and shows no opt-in. Only when an administrator starts the Pro trial or buys nexya Pro from the plugin’s screens are the site address, the WordPress, PHP and plugin versions and the administrator’s name and e-mail address sent to Freemius, which handles the checkout and the licence. Terms: https://freemius.com/terms/ — Privacy: https://freemius.com/privacy/

Lists of known hosts (Cookies and Security modules). These are not remote files and nothing is loaded from them. The cookie module carries a list of third-party hostnames (Google Fonts, Font Awesome, public CDNs, YouTube, Google Maps and so on) as plain data: a script or frame already on your page whose address matches one of them is held back until the visitor consents. The Security module carries a similar list of well-known origins, offered as ready-made lines when you write your site’s content security policy, the header that tells browsers which origins your pages may load from. Both lists are plain data files, modules/Cookie/data/hosts.json and modules/Security/data/origins.json. The plugin itself never contacts any of these hosts.

Requests to your own site. The cookie scan, the sharing-image finder of the SEO module and a few background jobs fetch pages of your own site from your own server. Nothing leaves it.

Third-party libraries

  • Chart.js 4.5.1 (MIT) draws the statistics charts — assets/js/chart.min.js. Source: https://github.com/chartjs/Chart.js
  • Freemius SDK (GPL) handles the licence and the update checks. Source: https://github.com/Freemius/wordpress-sdk
  • Font Awesome Free 6.7.2 brand icons (CC BY 4.0) for the social networks of e-mails and pop-ups — assets/social/. Source: https://fontawesome.com

The plugin’s own JavaScript and CSS ship as written, next to a minified copy of each file (.min.js / .min.css, made with esbuild when the plugin is packaged). The minified copies are loaded on the site; with SCRIPT_DEBUG on, the readable files are loaded instead.
sections.installation:
1. In Plugins > Add New, search for “freexya”, then install and activate it. You can also upload the folder to wp-content/plugins/.
  2. Open nexya in the admin menu. On a new install, a first card asks what kind of site this is — a showcase site, a shop or a blog — and switches on the modules that suit it in one click. You can also pick them yourself.
  3. The hub lists every module with its switch: a module that is off registers nothing on the site. Each module that is on gets its own page in the nexya menu, with its settings.
  4. The hub’s other tabs hold what is shared: Settings (the panel language, and whether your settings are kept if the plugin is deleted), Colours (your brand colours for the cookie banner, forms, messages and holding pages), AI (the connector the AI features use) and Export & import (every setting in one file, to copy a set-up to another site).
sections.faq:
Does a module I turned off still cost anything?

Almost nothing. The registry declares them all, but only boots the modules that are on: the others register no hooks, load no assets and run no queries.

Where are SMTP passwords stored?

Encrypted with AES-256-GCM in a single option, under a key derived from your WordPress salts. If you rotate those salts the stored secrets can no longer be read, and the panel tells you to enter them again.

And the licence?

The licence is handled by Freemius: the key, its activation and the checkout live in the Freemius screens under the nexya menu. The plugin stores nothing about it.

What happens when I uninstall?

You choose, when you deactivate the plugin (or in Settings › If the plugin is deleted):

  • Keep my settings — its scheduled tasks are cleared and the server rules it wrote are taken out; everything else stays, for a reinstall or a move to nexya Pro.
  • Erase everything — roles go back to the capabilities they had before the plugin touched them, the plugin’s tables and options are dropped, its scheduled tasks are cleared and the private folder is removed. A copy of the settings only (no logs, no page data) stays for 30 days as a WordPress transient, which WordPress deletes on its own once it expires; if the plugin comes back within that time, it offers to import it.

Can I move from WPML or Polylang?

Yes, in Translate › Import, after a backup and ideally on a copy of the site first. Languages, versions of contents, terms, menus, strings and forms come over; the former plugin is only switched off, so switching it back on restores the site. The addresses keep their shape, and those that change are redirected (301) through the Redirects module.

Not taken over: prices per currency from WooCommerce Multilingual, a domain or subdomain per language (redirect it at the host), translated media files, and add-ons that need WPML or Polylang themselves. Image alternative texts are translated in Texts › Images.

How do I move to nexya Pro without losing my settings?

Install and activate nexya Pro while this plugin is still in place: both read the same settings, and Pro switches this version off. Then delete this version.

  • Security: a plugin or theme updated through WordPress no longer shows up as changed files in the fingerprint, and every list of reported files has an Allow them all button.
  • Checkout (nexya Pro): a logged-in customer who has already ordered goes straight to the payment step, from the side cart or the checkout, with every step still one click away.
  • Checkout: the side cart shows a dark and a light button, the light one with colours of its own, and no longer a Continue shopping link under them.
  • Checkout: the privacy policy link of the payment step kept the theme’s blue.
  • SEO (nexya Pro): “Generate with AI” for the sharing image failed with “No models found” on a connector that cannot draw a wide image; the image is now asked in the widest format the connector draws, and a connector that only writes says so plainly.

1.4.3

  • Invoices (nexya Pro): invoices, receipts, delivery notes, packing slips and credit notes in PDF for every WooCommerce order, built section by section with a live preview, numbered in order, kept as issued, attached to the e-mails you choose and downloadable in My account.
  • Invoices: the Swiss QR-bill at the bottom of the invoice, with a QR-IBAN or an IBAN, the layout for window envelopes, a watermark, and printing in bulk from the list of orders.

1.4.2

  • Security: the content security policy, once confirmed, was missing on pages served from the cache; it now goes into the .htaccess block with the other headers.

1.4.1

  • Settings: a Test tab checks the site itself — security, e-mail, sharing and speed — and gives each test a grade from A to E, with what to fix.
  • Security: pages served from the cache went out without the security headers, the headers block and the cache blocks overwriting each other in the .htaccess; the block now has a name of its own and comes back by itself when it goes missing.
  • Checkout: the side cart opened on a reloaded page after an add to cart could show the cart as empty.

1.4.0

  • Checkout (nexya Pro): the WooCommerce checkout on a page of its own, in steps, with the order summary beside it, a look of its own set with a live preview, and a matching thank-you page.

  • Checkout: country, canton, date and phone code chosen in a small window; the town filled in from the postcode in eight countries; e-mail typos caught; phone numbers checked and stored in the international format; UID numbers checked; a delivery date and a pickup note.
  • Checkout: custom fields above the order notes, free or taken from an ACF or NCF product field, shown only when a product of the cart needs them; the answers are kept on the order and shown in the e-mails and on the thank-you page.
  • Checkout: a reminder for abandoned carts, an account created in one click after the order, the order’s progress, a review request, and the checkout funnel in Aris.
  • Captcha: WooCommerce orders were refused as coming from a robot, WooCommerce ticking the payment method again by script; a refused submission now says why.
  • Custom fields leave the beta.
  • Forms: the date picker takes a first and a last date.
  • WordPress.org: the plugin no longer preloads WordPress’s update data, which the Plugin Check took for an update routine.

1.3.11

  • Translation: the hreflang links are printed again. The module took its own Polylang compatibility functions for Polylang itself and stayed silent, on every site using it.

1.3.10

  • Interface: module headers, menu entries and tabs follow the admin’s language — French, German, Spanish or Italian — instead of English names.
  • Speed: CSS and JavaScript are served minified, the readable files staying in the plugin for SCRIPT_DEBUG; more settings are preloaded, and custom fields are no longer read for menus, images and styles, which have none: fewer queries on every page.

  • Translate: the language and the other versions of each content come from one index, read in a single query per page, instead of two queries for each linked content; the menu pre-reading of 1.2.38 is no longer needed and is gone.

Earlier versions: https://nexya.dev/en/whats-new/

short_description: Cookie consent with Google Consent Mode, SMTP with mail log, redirects and 404s, captcha, security headers — one light plugin, modules you switch on.
description:
One plugin for the jobs every WordPress site needs, instead of five or six:

  • E-mails that do not arrive — send through SMTP or an API, keep a log of every message, and read the server’s own reason when one fails.
  • A cookie banner that really blocks — third-party scripts and embeds wait for consent, with Google Consent Mode v2.
  • 404s after a redesign — a log of the broken addresses visitors hit, with their count, redirected in one click.
  • Security — HTTP headers, a limit on failed logins, and your plugins checked against known vulnerabilities.

Each job is a module you switch on from the hub, and a module that is off registers nothing: none of its hooks run on the site. The modules:

  • Dashboard — a readable admin home and a tidied toolbar.
  • Shortcuts — duplicate content, reorder it by hand, add entries in one click.
  • Roles & capabilities — capabilities sorted under the post type that creates them, and the site seen through a role’s eyes without leaving your own account.
  • Activity log — who changed what, with the before and the after.
  • Cookies — a consent banner, third-party scripts held back until consent, and a scan that finds them.
  • SEO — titles and descriptions with a suggestion drawn from the page’s text, sitemap, schema, llms.txt.
  • Mail — SMTP, an API provider, or a Gmail or Microsoft 365 account connected with OAuth, a delivery log, a test message, an invisible captcha for the site’s forms.
  • Redirects — exact redirects and a 404 log with the hit count.
  • Media — regenerate thumbnails in the background, in batches.
  • Security — security headers, a content policy, a limit on failed logins, and a check of the installed plugins against known vulnerabilities.
  • Maintenance — a holding page, database clean-up, a database export, and the previous version of each extension kept before its update.
  • Custom fields — field groups with repeaters, flexible content and relations, kept in their own tables, and content types and taxonomies of your own.
  • Element — sixteen Elementor widgets for custom fields, NCF’s or ACF’s: repeaters as cards, tabs or tables, galleries and sliders, key figures, teams, timelines, taxonomies, maps.
  • Translate — your site in several languages: each page linked to its translations, a translation editor beside the original (blocks, Elementor, ACF and NCF fields), addresses in /en/, a menu per language, a language switcher, hreflang, and every text of the site translated from the admin. A site coming from WPML or Polylang moves over in one click.

Free and Pro

Everything above is free, on as many sites as you like. nexya Pro, sold on nexya.dev, adds three modules — nexya forms, Mailya for newsletters and a page cache — and the parts that do the repetitive work for you: suggested redirects and pattern rules, CSV import, a daily vulnerability pass and a file fingerprint with rollback, a two-step login, updates undone by themselves when they break the site, undo from the activity log, a second sending server and failure alerts for mail, a branded login screen and admin skin, banner appearance and consent service by service, scheduled database clean-up, orphan image sizes, folders in the media library, and longer log retention. The free version contains none of that code; nexya Pro is delivered by Freemius after purchase, and takes over from this plugin with the same settings.

Privacy

The plugin sends nothing to a third party by default. The features that reach the network, and what they send, are listed under External services below.

Multisite

Multisite networks are not supported. On a network the plugin stays switched off and says so.

External services

Nothing below runs unless you switch the matching module or option on. No data leaves the site by default, and the plugin sends no usage data anywhere.

WPVulnerability (Security module, vulnerability watch). When you start a check from the Security screen, the plugin asks the public WPVulnerability API whether the installed plugins have known vulnerabilities. For each installed plugin, its slug is sent to www.wpvulnerability.net; nothing else about the site is sent. Nothing is sent until you start a check. Terms and privacy (legal notice of its publisher): https://www.robotstxt.es/legal/

WordPress.org checksums (Security module). While the Security module is on, once a day and when you press “Check now”, the plugin asks api.wordpress.org — the same service WordPress uses for its own updates — for the checksums of the installed WordPress version, sending only that version number and the site language, then compares them with the core files on your server. Terms: https://wordpress.org/about/privacy/

IndexNow (SEO module, optional, off by default). Only if you switch it on, each time a page is published, updated or taken down its address is sent to api.indexnow.org, which shares it with the search engines that take part (Bing, Yandex, Seznam, Naver and others), along with the site’s host name and the verification key the plugin serves at the root of your site. Nothing is sent while the site asks search engines not to index it, or runs on a local address. Terms: https://www.indexnow.org/terms — Privacy (Microsoft, which runs the IndexNow service): https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/privacy/privacystatement

Stripe (nexya forms, Payment module, optional, nexya Pro). Only once you switch the module on and enter your own Stripe secret key, a form with a payment field sends, when the visitor submits it, the amount, the currency, the name of the form, the visitor’s e-mail address if the form asks for one, and the entry’s number to api.stripe.com to open a Stripe Checkout page; the visitor then pays on Stripe’s site. Stripe calls back the site’s own webhook address to confirm the payment. Terms: https://stripe.com/legal/ssa — Privacy: https://stripe.com/privacy

PayPal (nexya forms, Payment module, optional, nexya Pro). Only once you enter your own PayPal REST app credentials, a form with a payment field sends, when the visitor chooses PayPal, the amount, the currency, the name of the form and the entry’s number to api-m.paypal.com (or api-m.sandbox.paypal.com in sandbox mode) to open a PayPal approval page; the visitor approves the payment on PayPal’s site, and the site captures it when they come back. Terms: https://www.paypal.com/legalhub/home — Privacy: https://www.paypal.com/myaccount/privacy/privacyhub

Patchstack (Security module, optional). Only if you enter your own Patchstack API key, the same check also asks api.patchstack.com, sending each installed plugin’s slug and your key. Terms: https://patchstack.com/terms-and-conditions/ — Privacy: https://patchstack.com/privacy-policy/

E-mail delivery (E-mails module). When you pick an API provider instead of SMTP, the messages your site sends are handed to that provider’s API: sender, recipients, subject, body and attachments, at the moment the message is sent. You choose the provider and enter its API key. The providers offered are Brevo (https://www.brevo.com/legal/termsofuse/ — https://www.brevo.com/legal/privacypolicy/), SendGrid (https://www.twilio.com/en-us/legal/tos — https://www.twilio.com/en-us/legal/privacy), Postmark (https://postmarkapp.com/terms-of-service — https://postmarkapp.com/privacy-policy), Resend (https://resend.com/legal/terms-of-service — https://resend.com/legal/privacy-policy), SMTP2GO (https://www.smtp2go.com/terms/ — https://www.smtp2go.com/privacy/), MailerSend (https://www.mailersend.com/legal/terms-of-service — https://www.mailersend.com/legal/privacy-policy), SendLayer (https://sendlayer.com/terms-of-service/ — https://sendlayer.com/privacy-policy/), Mandrill (https://mailchimp.com/legal/terms/ — https://mailchimp.com/legal/privacy/), Mailgun (https://www.mailgun.com/legal/terms/ — https://www.mailgun.com/legal/privacy-policy/), Elastic Email (https://elasticemail.com/resources/usage-policies/terms-of-use — https://elasticemail.com/resources/usage-policies/privacy-policy) and SparkPost (https://www.sparkpost.com/policies/tou/ — https://www.sparkpost.com/policies/privacy/).

Gmail and Microsoft 365 sending (E-mails module, optional). Only if you choose Google (Gmail, Workspace) or Microsoft 365 (Outlook) as the sending method and connect an account. When you press “Connect”, your browser goes to accounts.google.com or login.microsoftonline.com, where you sign in and allow the site to send e-mail; the plugin then sends the authorisation code it gets back, with the client ID and secret you entered, to oauth2.googleapis.com or login.microsoftonline.com to obtain an access token, and renews that token there when it expires while the site is sending. No password is stored on the site. Each message the site sends then goes through smtp.gmail.com, or smtp.office365.com / smtp-mail.outlook.com, with its sender, recipients, subject, body and attachments, at the moment it is sent. Google — Terms: https://policies.google.com/terms — Privacy: https://policies.google.com/privacy. Microsoft — Terms: https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/servicesagreement — Privacy: https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/privacy/privacystatement

Cloudflare (Cache module, optional). Only if you switch the Cloudflare option on and enter your zone ID and API token: each time the nexya cache is emptied, the plugin asks api.cloudflare.com to empty the cache of that zone, sending the zone ID, the token and, when only some pages changed, their addresses. Terms: https://www.cloudflare.com/terms/ — Privacy: https://www.cloudflare.com/privacypolicy/

Form webhook (nexya forms, optional). Only if you enter an address in a form’s settings, each entry of that form is sent, when it is submitted, to that address as JSON: the form’s name and number, the entry’s number and date, the page it was sent from, the site’s address, and the answers with the label and type of each field. You choose the address (Zapier, Make, n8n, a CRM…); the plugin contacts no address you did not enter, and the terms and privacy policy that apply are those of the service you chose.

AI suggestions (optional). The plugin calls no AI provider itself. When you press a button that asks for a suggestion (a title, a description, an image text…), the text needed for it is handed to the AI client built into WordPress, which sends it to the provider of the connector you set up in WordPress, under that provider’s terms. Without such a connector, these buttons do not appear and nothing is sent.

Audience measurement tags (SEO module). If, and only if, you enter an ID or an address for one of them, the module prints that service’s tag on the front end; the visitor’s browser then loads the script from the service and sends it what that tag collects.
* Google Tag Manager and Google Analytics 4, from www.googletagmanager.com. Terms: https://marketingplatform.google.com/about/analytics/terms/us/ — Privacy: https://policies.google.com/privacy
* Plausible, from plausible.io or the address you enter. Terms: https://plausible.io/terms — Privacy: https://plausible.io/privacy
* Umami, from the address of your own Umami instance or Umami Cloud. Terms: https://umami.is/terms — Privacy: https://umami.is/privacy
* Matomo, from the address of your own Matomo instance or Matomo Cloud. Terms: https://matomo.org/matomo-cloud-terms-of-service/ — Privacy: https://matomo.org/privacy-policy/

Freemius (trial and purchase of nexya Pro). The Freemius SDK ships with the plugin in anonymous mode: on its own it sends nothing and shows no opt-in. Only when an administrator starts the Pro trial or buys nexya Pro from the plugin’s screens are the site address, the WordPress, PHP and plugin versions and the administrator’s name and e-mail address sent to Freemius, which handles the checkout and the licence. Terms: https://freemius.com/terms/ — Privacy: https://freemius.com/privacy/

Lists of known hosts (Cookies and Security modules). These are not remote files and nothing is loaded from them. The cookie module carries a list of third-party hostnames (Google Fonts, Font Awesome, public CDNs, YouTube, Google Maps and so on) as plain data: a script or frame already on your page whose address matches one of them is held back until the visitor consents. The Security module carries a similar list of well-known origins, offered as ready-made lines when you write your site’s content security policy, the header that tells browsers which origins your pages may load from. Both lists are plain data files, modules/Cookie/data/hosts.json and modules/Security/data/origins.json. The plugin itself never contacts any of these hosts.

Requests to your own site. The cookie scan, the sharing-image finder of the SEO module and a few background jobs fetch pages of your own site from your own server. Nothing leaves it.

Third-party libraries

  • Chart.js 4.5.1 (MIT) draws the statistics charts — assets/js/chart.min.js. Source: https://github.com/chartjs/Chart.js
  • Freemius SDK (GPL) handles the licence and the update checks. Source: https://github.com/Freemius/wordpress-sdk
  • Font Awesome Free 6.7.2 brand icons (CC BY 4.0) for the social networks of e-mails and pop-ups — assets/social/. Source: https://fontawesome.com

The plugin’s own JavaScript and CSS ship as written, next to a minified copy of each file (.min.js / .min.css, made with esbuild when the plugin is packaged). The minified copies are loaded on the site; with SCRIPT_DEBUG on, the readable files are loaded instead.
